in_context.text: This is the closing line of the elder's short letter to Gaius. Rather than write more with ink and pen, he hopes to come soon and talk in person. He ends with a wish of peace and greetings passed between friends.

speaker.text: "The elder," the unnamed writer of the letter. Early Christian tradition identifies him as John the apostle.

audience.text: Gaius, a believer the elder loves and counts among his children in the faith.

affected.text: "Our friends" with the elder send greetings, and Gaius is asked to greet "the friends" where he is, each by name.

what.text: The elder says he hopes to see Gaius shortly and speak with him face to face. He wishes him peace, sends greetings from friends, and asks Gaius to greet the friends by name.

events.text: The visit is still in the future. The elder hopes it will be soon, and earlier he says that "if I come" he will deal with Diotrephes.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 85-95, around the time of 1 and 2 John. Scholarly view: most also place it in the late first century, though some think "the elder" was a church leader other than the apostle.

where.text: The letter does not say where it was written. Early tradition places John's last years in Ephesus. Gaius lived near a church the elder had written to before, likely in the province of Asia.

purpose.text: The elder keeps the rest of what he has to say for an in-person meeting. This ties in with his plan to come and address the trouble caused by Diotrephes.

big_picture.text: Wishing peace and passing on greetings was a common way to close letters among believers. Paul and Peter do the same.

for_readers.text: The verse shows a church leader who values personal presence and knows people by name. Faith here is lived out in real friendships, not only in written words.

why_it_matters.text: The word means to look for, expect or hope. The lexicon lists this same use, "hope" followed by a verb, for travel plans in 2 John 12, Philippians 2:19 and 1 Corinthians 16:7. So "I trust" here expresses a hoped-for visit, not a firm promise.
The word is glossed "immediately" and defined as straightway, at once, directly. It shows that the elder hoped to come very soon.

"Face to face" is literally "mouth to mouth." The lexicon links the phrase to the Hebrew expression in Numbers 12:8 and treats the mouth here as the organ of speech. The stress falls on talking together in person.

takeaway.text: This is a warm, personal farewell. The elder hopes to visit soon, wishes Gaius peace, and sends greetings to friends by name. Some things are better said in person than in writing.
